opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that token selection in sparse attention is a really hard credit-assignment problem if you try to learn it from scratch. The selection step is usually discrete, like a top-k over blocks or tokens, so gradients don't flow through the choice itself. If the model picks the wrong blocks, it never sees what it missed. It only gets a weak, indirect signal from the language-modeling loss, and that signal is very noisy, especially early in training.

Distillation changes that. If you have a dense-attention teacher, either a separate model or the same model running full attention, its attention distribution is basically a map of where the important information is. So instead of the sparse model guessing and slowly correcting itself through the LM loss, you directly supervise the indexer or router: "these are the keys the full attention actually put mass on, so learn to score them highly." It turns a sparse reward problem into dense, token-level supervision.

There's also a nice empirical property here. Attention in trained models is already quite sparse in practice. A small fraction of keys usually carries most of the probability mass. So the teacher's signal is learnable: you're not asking a lightweight selector to approximate something arbitrary, you're asking it to find a fairly concentrated set of positions. That's why you can often use a very cheap scorer, low-dimensional and maybe low-precision, and still get high recall on the tokens that matter.

And practically, it helps stability. A common recipe is to start from a dense model, warm up the selector by aligning it with the dense attention distribution, using something like a KL loss, and only then switch to truly sparse training. If you go sparse from the beginning, the selector and the main attention can co-adapt in bad ways. The selector picks some tokens, attention learns to live with them, and you lock in a suboptimal pattern. Distillation anchors the selector to what full attention would have wanted before that feedback loop sets in.

So I'd summarize it this way: distillation gives the discrete selection step a direct, dense, and well-defined target, and attention's natural sparsity makes that target easy to match with a cheap selector.

r001.rationale: The response says discrete selection blocks gradients through the choice, so wrong picks receive only a weak, noisy indirect language-modeling signal.

r002.rationale: It explains that a dense-attention teacher guides token selection, but does not clearly identify that teacher as pretrained.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the cleanest way to say it is that selection is a hard problem to learn from scratch, because the training signal for "which tokens matter" is extremely indirect.

Think about what a sparse attention layer has to do. It has a selector that decides which blocks or tokens get attended to, and then the actual attention only runs over that subset. If you train this end to end from random initialization, the only feedback the selector gets is through the language modeling loss, and that signal has to pass through a discrete or near-discrete choice. Early in training the selector is basically guessing, the attention sees garbage, the loss is high, and it's very hard to attribute blame back to "you should have picked that block over there." So you get this chicken-and-egg problem: the attention can't learn good representations without good selection, and the selector can't learn good selection without informative attention.

Distillation breaks that loop. If you have a dense teacher, you already have something that knows, for every query, how the attention mass is actually distributed. That's a direct, dense supervision signal for exactly the thing the selector is trying to approximate. Instead of inferring importance from a scalar loss, you can tell the selector: here's the full attention distribution, match its top-k, or match the per-block mass. That's a much better conditioned learning problem.

There's also a second, subtler effect. The dense teacher's attention patterns are usually fairly structured. Most of the mass sits on a small number of positions, and those patterns are consistent across layers and heads in ways that a sparse model can realistically reproduce. So you're not asking the student to learn arbitrary sparsity, you're asking it to learn the specific sparsity that already exists in a well-trained dense model. That's a lot more achievable, and it also means you don't lose much quality, because you're approximating something that was already nearly sparse.

And practically, it lets you decouple the two stages. You can initialize from a dense checkpoint, keep the value and output pathways largely intact, and spend your compute specifically on teaching the selection mechanism. From an engineering standpoint that's much more stable than hoping sparse attention discovers the right routing on its own at scale. People have tried the from-scratch route, and it tends to work only when the sparsity pattern is very constrained, like sliding windows or fixed strides. Once you want learned, content-dependent selection, having a teacher to copy from is the thing that makes it reliable.

r001.rationale: The response says the from-scratch selector receives only an indirect language-modeling signal through a discrete or near-discrete choice, making it difficult to attribute feedback and learn correct selections. This conveys unreliable learning feedback as the reason.

r002.rationale: It explains that a dense teacher provides the teacher's attention distribution as direct supervision, guiding the sparse selector to match top-k tokens or per-block attention mass.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps because token selection is a credit assignment problem. If you train sparse attention only with the final language modeling loss, the selector gets a fairly indirect signal: the prediction was wrong, but which token should it have kept? And once a token is excluded, it’s harder to learn what that token could have contributed.

A dense attention teacher gives you a richer signal because it can see all the tokens. You can use its attention patterns or its outputs to guide the sparse model toward the information that matters. So instead of discovering both how to select tokens and how to use them from scratch, the sparse model learns to preserve the useful behavior of the dense model under a smaller attention budget.

That doesn’t mean the teacher’s attention weights are perfect importance labels. But they can provide a much more direct training signal than the final loss alone.

r001.rationale: The response says the final language-modeling loss gives an indirect selector signal, but does not identify unreliable gradients as the reason sparse attention may fail to select the correct blocks.

r002.rationale: It explains that a dense attention teacher can guide token selection using its attention patterns or outputs, but does not say the teacher is pretrained.

sol-6.1.text:
I think distillation helps because token selection is a difficult thing to learn from the final language-model loss alone. If the model makes a bad selection, that loss doesn’t clearly tell the selector which important token it missed. A dense-attention teacher provides a more direct signal: for each query, it shows which tokens receive attention. The sparse selector can learn to preserve those important connections with a limited budget.

So you’re giving the selector a useful target instead of asking it to discover everything indirectly. It doesn’t need to reproduce the full attention distribution perfectly; it mainly needs to identify the tokens that matter most.

r001.rationale: The response explains that final language-model loss does not clearly tell the selector which important tokens it missed, conveying unreliable learning signals as a reason selection can fail.

r002.rationale: It says a dense-attention teacher guides token selection, but does not identify the teacher as pretrained.
